meta.name: CWNA-108 Certified Wireless Network Administrator
meta.notes: Initial authoring pass. Covers all seven CWNA-108 domains: RF technologies, WLAN regulations and standards, WLAN protocols and devices, WLAN network architecture, WLAN network security, RF validation and troubleshooting, and RF site survey. Correct positions distributed across A/B/C/D.

questions.question: An access point radiates 20 dBm at its connector, is fed through a cable with 3 dB of loss, and connects to an antenna with 6 dBi of gain. What is the EIRP in the direction of the antenna's main lobe?
options: A. 17 dBm
B. 23 dBm
C. 26 dBm
D. 29 dBm
questions.explanation: EIRP is transmitter output minus cable losses plus antenna gain: 20 dBm - 3 dB + 6 dBi = 23 dBm. Option A subtracts the antenna gain instead of adding it. Option C ignores the cable loss (20 + 6 = 26). Option D adds all three magnitudes with the wrong sign on the cable (20 + 3 + 6 = 29). EIRP is a regulatory ceiling in many regions, so remembering to apply cable loss as a subtraction is central to legal deployment planning.

questions.question: A Wi-Fi engineer wants the widest set of non-overlapping 20 MHz channels available for a dense indoor deployment in the United States. Which band should they primarily plan into?
options: B. 5 GHz UNII-1 only
C. 5 GHz UNII-1 through UNII-3 including the DFS sub-bands
D. 900 MHz ISM
questions.explanation: In the United States the 5 GHz band across UNII-1, UNII-2, UNII-2 Extended and UNII-3 exposes roughly 25 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels once the DFS sub-bands are enabled, which is what dense enterprise designs rely on. The 2.4 GHz band offers only three non-overlapping 20 MHz channels (1, 6, 11) and is unsuitable for dense reuse. UNII-1 alone contributes four channels, far fewer than the full 5 GHz range. The 900 MHz ISM band is used by IoT radios such as LoRa, not 802.11 Wi-Fi certified for CWNA.

questions.question: Which 802.11 frame subtype must a station successfully exchange with an access point before it can send data frames through that BSS?
options: A. Probe Request
B. Beacon
C. Association Request and Response
D. RTS/CTS
questions.explanation: A station moves through discovery, authentication, and finally association; only after the Association Request has been accepted with an Association Response is the station a member of the BSS and permitted to send data frames. Probe Requests are used during discovery. Beacons are advertisements sourced by the AP and are not exchanged with the client. RTS/CTS is an optional control-frame handshake for medium reservation and does not create membership in a BSS.

questions.question: In an 802.11 half-duplex medium, which access method do stations use to reduce the probability of collisions on the wireless channel?
options: A. CSMA/CD with backoff after collision detection
B. Token passing coordinated by the AP
C. TDMA slots assigned by the DHCP server
D. CSMA/CA with a random backoff inside the contention window
questions.explanation: 802.11 uses Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance: a station senses the medium, waits a DIFS interval, and then draws a random backoff slot from the contention window before transmitting, which spreads simultaneous attempts in time. CSMA/CD is the wired Ethernet method and does not apply because a half-duplex radio cannot listen while it transmits. Token passing is not used in 802.11 BSS. DHCP is a layer-3 address protocol and never allocates radio access slots.

questions.question: An enterprise WLAN requires per-user authentication tied to an existing corporate identity store. Which WPA2/WPA3 mode should the SSID be configured to use?
options: A. Personal mode with a shared passphrase (PSK or SAE)
B. Open authentication with a captive portal on the AP
C. WEP with a shared 128-bit key rotated monthly
D. Enterprise mode with 802.1X and an EAP method against a RADIUS server
questions.explanation: WPA2-Enterprise and WPA3-Enterprise use 802.1X to carry an EAP conversation between the supplicant, the authenticator (AP or controller) and a RADIUS server tied to the identity store, yielding unique per-user credentials and per-session keys. Personal mode uses one shared secret and cannot distinguish users. A captive portal over open authentication leaves the RF unencrypted and is a guest-access construct. WEP is deprecated, cryptographically broken, and never appropriate for enterprise identity binding.

questions.question: A Wi-Fi 6 access point advertises OFDMA support. What is the primary benefit OFDMA delivers over the OFDM scheme used by 802.11n and 802.11ac?
options: A. It doubles the maximum transmit power permitted per client.
B. It replaces CSMA/CA with a fully scheduled MAC layer.
C. It subdivides a channel into resource units so multiple clients can transmit in the same OFDM symbol.
D. It removes the need for channel bonding above 20 MHz.
questions.explanation: OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiple Access) partitions a 20/40/80/160 MHz channel into resource units of 26, 52, 106, 242+ tones, so the AP can serve several clients simultaneously in one PPDU rather than one client per symbol as classical OFDM did, which is especially effective for small frames in dense environments. Transmit power is unchanged by OFDMA. CSMA/CA still governs contention. Channel bonding remains available and orthogonal to OFDMA.

questions.question: A designer is planning coverage for a warehouse with tall metal racks and long, narrow aisles. Which antenna type most effectively steers energy down the aisles and away from the walls?
options: A. A high-gain patch or directional antenna aimed along the aisle
B. A rubber-duck omnidirectional antenna at each AP
C. A ceiling-mounted low-gain dipole
D. A parabolic dish antenna aimed at the roof deck
questions.explanation: Patch and other directional antennas concentrate energy into a defined beamwidth, which is exactly what long, narrow aisles need to keep RF along the aisle rather than reflecting off metal rack sides. Omnidirectional rubber-ducks and low-gain dipoles radiate in a doughnut pattern and waste energy into rack walls, creating multipath. A parabolic dish is very high gain and narrow beam, but aiming it at the roof deck would spray reflections rather than serve users on the floor.

questions.question: During a passive site survey the analyst walks the floor with the survey adapter listening only. What primary information does this survey type collect?
options: A. Client association counts and per-client throughput to each AP
B. TCP retransmission and jitter measurements between the client and a test server
C. RADIUS authentication success and failure counts by SSID
D. Received signal strength, noise floor, and SNR from beacons already in the air
questions.explanation: A passive survey records the RF that is already being transmitted, primarily beacons from every heard BSS, and measures RSSI, noise floor, SNR, channel utilization and co-channel interference at each map point. Association counts and throughput are not collected because the adapter never associates. Retransmission and jitter measurements require an active survey with a real associated link. RADIUS auth counts are logged at the AAA server, not by an RF adapter.

questions.question: Which statement about SSID, BSSID and ESSID in an 802.11 infrastructure network is correct?
options: A. The ESSID is the roaming domain shared by APs advertising the same SSID; the BSSID is the MAC-address identifier of one specific radio.
B. The BSSID is a 32-character human-readable name; the SSID is the AP's MAC address.
C. The SSID is a 48-bit identifier equal to the client's MAC address for that association.
D. The BSSID changes each time a client roams to a new AP but the client's MAC address remains constant.
questions.explanation: The SSID is the network name (up to 32 octets). The BSSID is the 48-bit MAC-format identifier of a single AP radio interface. An ESS is a set of BSSs sharing the same SSID across a common distribution system, and its identifier (ESSID) is that shared SSID which enables client roaming. Option B is wrong about which value is the human-readable name and which is the MAC-format value. Option C swaps the SSID for the client's own MAC. Option D is inverted: as the client roams, the BSSID it associates to does change because it is the AP's identifier, but that alone does not describe how SSID/BSSID/ESSID relate.

questions.question: A troubleshooter observes that clients on a 5 GHz DFS channel occasionally disconnect for several seconds after which the AP appears on a different channel. What is the most likely cause?
options: A. The AP's radio has failed a hardware self-test and rebooted.
B. The AP detected a radar pulse and executed a channel move as required by DFS regulations.
C. The controller pushed a firmware upgrade to that AP.
D. WPA3 SAE re-authentication forced a channel change.
questions.explanation: Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) on 5 GHz UNII-2 and UNII-2e sub-bands requires that when an AP detects a radar pattern it vacate the channel within the regulator-specified timer (typically 10 seconds in most regions) and remain off that channel for a non-occupancy period. Clients see this as a brief outage followed by the BSS appearing on a new channel. Radio hardware faults would not respect DFS timing patterns. Firmware upgrades take much longer than a few seconds and are scheduled, not spontaneous. WPA3 SAE re-authenticates keys but never changes the operating channel.

questions.question: A high-density stadium design uses 40 MHz channel width on 5 GHz APs. As channel width doubles from 20 to 40 MHz, what happens to the noise floor and to the number of non-overlapping channels available for reuse?
options: A. Noise floor rises about 3 dB and the number of non-overlapping channels is roughly halved.
B. Noise floor drops about 3 dB and the number of non-overlapping channels doubles.
C. Noise floor is unchanged and the number of non-overlapping channels doubles.
D. Noise floor rises about 10 dB and the number of non-overlapping channels stays the same.
questions.explanation: Wider channels admit more thermal noise, so doubling bandwidth from 20 to 40 MHz raises the effective noise floor by approximately 3 dB (10*log10(2)). It also consumes twice the spectrum per BSS, roughly halving how many non-overlapping channels remain for cell reuse, which is why very dense stadium and lecture-hall designs often revert to 20 MHz. B and C invert both effects. D overstates the noise increase (10 dB would be a ten-fold bandwidth increase, not two-fold).

questions.question: Which improvement does WPA3-Personal (SAE) provide over WPA2-Personal (PSK) even when both use the same passphrase?
options: A. SAE eliminates the need for the passphrase entirely once the first client has connected.
B. SAE is resistant to offline dictionary attack on the captured handshake, whereas WPA2-PSK's 4-way handshake is offline-crackable.
C. SAE replaces AES-CCMP with plaintext transmission for latency reasons.
D. SAE runs only on Wi-Fi 6E 6 GHz radios and cannot be used on 2.4 or 5 GHz.
questions.explanation: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) replaces the WPA2 PSK 4-way handshake with a Dragonfly-based key exchange that provides forward secrecy and makes captured handshakes computationally infeasible to brute-force offline; that resistance to offline dictionary attack is the headline security gain. WPA3 still requires the passphrase for every association. It continues to use AES-based frame encryption (CCMP-128 or GCMP-256) rather than plaintext. SAE is available on 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz radios, though 6E mandates it.
